chunks: And a woman asked him: There is menstrual blood on my garment, and I washed it, but its trace did not go away. So he said: “Dye it with mishq.”

Then he said, may Allah the Exalted support him: If a person has sores whose blood continually oozes, there is no hardship upon him regarding salat (prayer) in respect of what of that blood reaches the garments, even if it is much. Likewise, if he has wounds that ooze, and their blood and pus reach his garment, then he may pray in the garment even if that becomes much in it.
What indicates this is His, the Exalted’s, saying: “He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship.”

And we know that if the legally responsible person were obligated to remove the blood from these things inseparable from him, he would be put into hardship by that, and burden and difficulty would befall him because of it, and perhaps salat (prayer) would also pass him by along with that. So Allah the Exalted permitted that out of care for His servants and compassion toward them; and this is also indicated from the standpoint of the report.
33 — And this hadith was narrated from Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā ibn ʿUbayd, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā al-Ashʿarī; and he added in it:

key_terms.بُثُورٌ: sores or eruptions on the body
key_terms.حَرَجٍ: hardship or undue difficulty in religious duty
key_terms.ٱلصَّلَاةِ: salat (prayer), whose validity is under discussion

ai.seo_question: Can a person pray in clothes stained with blood from ongoing wounds or sores if removing it causes hardship?
ai.summary: This passage gives a legal ruling on impurity in garments used for salat (prayer), distinguishing between removable traces and ongoing conditions that cause continuous bleeding or discharge. It grounds the concession in the Qur’anic principle that Allah has not placed hardship in the religion, showing legal ease for cases of persistent wounds and sores.
